Sourcing guide · September 16, 2026 · 6 min read

How logo decoration on barware and drinkware is specified

What to send, what decides feasibility, and what has to be approved before a branded run starts — without assuming one method fits every material.

Start from the artwork, not from the method

The single biggest cause of a late branded order is artwork that cannot be produced as supplied. Send the logo as vector artwork — AI, EPS or PDF with the text converted to outlines — and state the Pantone reference for each colour. That gives a decoration area that can be measured and a colour that can be matched, instead of a screenshot that has to be redrawn.

If only a raster file exists, we confirm whether it can be reproduced cleanly at the size the item allows. A redraw is a separate step and belongs in the schedule, not in the week the goods were supposed to ship.

Decoration area and colour count decide feasibility

The available decoration area follows the surface of the selected item. A tall flute and a short shot glass offer very different usable areas, and a curved surface reduces the area that will reproduce cleanly compared with a flat panel. This is why we confirm feasibility against the exact SKU rather than approving a logo across a whole range.

Colour count changes both cost and feasibility. Each additional colour on a printed mark adds a setup and a pass, and on a moulded or coated surface the substrate has to accept the ink reliably. Where a client wants four colours on a small curved area, the honest answer is often that the artwork needs simplifying for that item.

Choosing between a printed mark and a permanent mark

A printed mark is the lower-cost route and suits short runs, multi-colour artwork and flat or gently curved areas. An engraved mark is cut into the material rather than sitting on the surface, which matters for items that will be washed repeatedly or kept as a keepsake — the mark cannot wear off because it is not a layer.

Which methods are actually available depends on the material and the shape, so they are confirmed for the SKU you select. Engraving is not appropriate on every surface, and printing is not appropriate where the mark has to survive years of washing.

What has to be approved before production starts

The production brief is what the run is judged against, so it is approved as a whole: the SKU specification, the artwork, the logo position, the decoration method, the packaging build, the quantity and the destination.

Where the appearance is colour sensitive, a colour chip or a pre-production sample is approved before the bulk run. That step exists to protect both sides: it is far cheaper to reject a sample than to reject a container.

Care after decoration

The care instruction for a decorated item follows the material of the item. Warm soapy water and a soft cloth are appropriate for a printed mark; abrasive scouring pads and very hot cycles are not, because they attack the ink film rather than the item.

Where an item is expected to be washed by housekeeping or by a venue's glasswash operation every day, that is a reason to specify a permanent mark rather than a cheaper printed one.

Questions on this topic

What artwork file should I provide for a logo on drinkware or barware?

Vector artwork — AI, EPS or PDF with the text converted to outlines — plus the Pantone reference for each colour. If only a raster file exists, we confirm whether it reproduces cleanly at the size the selected item allows, and any redraw is scheduled as a separate step.

How do logo position and colour count affect decoration feasibility?

The available decoration area follows the surface of the selected SKU, and a curved surface reduces the area that prints cleanly compared with a flat panel. Each additional colour adds a setup and a pass, so colour count affects both cost and feasibility and is confirmed for the exact item.

When is laser engraving suitable, and when is printing the better route?

Engraving suits items that will be washed repeatedly or kept as a keepsake, because the mark is cut into the material rather than sitting on the surface. Printing suits short runs and multi-colour artwork where unit cost is the priority. Which methods apply is confirmed for the SKU and material you select.

What must be approved before branded production starts?

The SKU specification, the artwork, the logo position, the decoration method, the packaging build, the quantity and the final production brief. Where the appearance is colour sensitive, a colour chip or a pre-production sample is approved before the bulk run.

How should branded drinkware be cared for after decoration?

Follow the care instruction for the material of the item: warm soapy water and a soft cloth. Abrasive scouring pads and very hot cycles are not appropriate for a printed mark because they attack the ink film. Where an item is washed daily, specify a permanent mark.

Can you match a specific Pantone reference for the logo?

Colour is matched to the Pantone reference you supply, and where the appearance is colour sensitive a colour chip or pre-production sample is approved before the bulk run. The match is confirmed against the substrate of the selected SKU, because the same ink reads differently on a moulded surface and a coated one.

What happens if the artwork changes after it has been approved?

A change to approved artwork is treated as a new brief. The artwork, the decoration area and the proof are re-approved before production resumes, and a change to the method or the area is re-quoted.
